subject: Archaeology
title: Conservation: Saving What the Sea Gives Back
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Conservation: Saving What the Sea Gives Back.

hook.text: Pulling an artifact from the sea is easy. Keeping it from crumbling to dust afterward is the hard part.

buildup.text: Waterlogged wood shrinks and cracks when it dries. Metal corrodes rapidly once exposed to air after centuries.

discovery.text: The Vasa warship spent 17 years being sprayed with polyethylene glycol to replace water in its wood cells.

twist.text: Some objects are better left on the seabed. Raising them without proper facilities can destroy them faster than the sea.

climax.text: Conservation costs often exceed excavation costs. Many underwater finds wait years in water tanks for treatment.

punchline.text: Finding a wreck takes skill. Keeping it intact takes patience, chemistry, and years.

quiz.question: Why can raising artifacts from the sea actually damage them?
options: Sunlight bleaches all underwater pigments immediately
Waterlogged wood shrinks and metal corrodes rapidly once exposed to air
The change in water pressure causes artifacts to expand and crack

details.summary: Objects recovered from underwater environments begin to deteriorate immediately when exposed to air. Conservation science uses desalination, freeze-drying, chemical stabilization, and controlled environments to prevent artifacts from crumbling, warping, or corroding after centuries of stable.
details.whyItMatters: Without conservation, recovered artifacts self-destruct. The Vasa warship required 17 years of treatment with polyethylene glycol.
takeaways: Underwater artifacts deteriorate rapidly when exposed to air
Conservation uses desalination, freeze-drying, and chemical treatment
Without conservation, recovered objects would self-destruct

faq.question: Why do underwater objects deteriorate when recovered?
faq.answer: Waterlogged wood contains water in place of decayed cellulose — remove the water and the wood collapses. Iron objects form stable compounds underwater but rapidly corrode in air. Salt crystallization inside porous materials causes cracking. Each material requires different treatment.

faq.question: How long does conservation take?
faq.answer: Years to decades. The Mary Rose required continuous spraying with PEG for 19 years followed by controlled drying. Individual metal objects may need months of electrolytic treatment. Conservation is often the most time-consuming and expensive part of any underwater archaeology project.
